newsitem.title: USA: New Blockbuster chief seen boosting chain.
newsitem.headline: New Blockbuster chief seen boosting chain.

text.p: John Antioco, the new chief of Viacom Inc's Blockbuster Entertainment unit, has a reputation for turning around wobbly retail operations, the task he faces at the troubled video renter.

"In the retail business, you're trying to figure out what's going to drive customers into the stores, how to sell it to them, and make sure they come back frequently, and he's done that," said Steve Kernkraut, an analyst at Bear Stearns.
Viacom Tuesday named Antioco as chairman and chief executive officer of Blockbuster. He had served as president and chief executive officer of PepsiCo Inc's Taco Bell since last October.

Blockbuster, which operates about 5,300 video stores worldwide, including about 3,700 in the U.S., has suffered from a lack of direction and high costs, in part from buying movies, as well as an overall weaker line of new movies.
"Antioco's going to go back to basics," said David Doft, an analyst at Furman Selz. "He's going to focus on video rentals."
"He's known for his operational experience," Doft added. "That's something that Blockbuster needs right now."
Antioco's predecessor, Bill Fields, a former Wal-Mart Stores Inc executive, left Blockbuster in April, after an apparent conflict with Viacom managers over Blockbuster's strategic direction.

Analysts said that Fields sought to turn Blockbuster units from neighborhood video stores into entertainment centers, selling licensed merchandise and music as well as so-called impulse items like soft drinks and candy.
That strategy was based on his experience at Wal-Mart, a so-called big-box store, compared to Blockbuster, a small box.
Fields also sought to maintain larger inventories as part of a strategy of carrying more new releases in larger volume.
"That strategy didn't work in a small box," said Doft, in part because the non-video items had lower margins.
Blockbuster is now focusing more on video rentals, considered a high-margin business. Blockbuster is also pulling back from selling lower-priced videos.
Analysts said Antioco's star rose at Circle K Corp, which he joined in 1991.
As chief executive, he led the company out of Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection, building up the chain to 2,500 stores. Circle K was sold to Tosco Corp last year.
"He was an excellent guy in running Circle K," said Kernkraut. "I have a high regard for him. He's a seasoned executive."
"He's a people person, who surrounds himself with experts who come up with a strategic plan, and then executes it," Kernkraut added.
"He turned around the company," said Doft. "He has a great reputation in the retail business, and has a strong operations background."

William Franke, who was on the Circle K board that hired Antioco and is currently chairman of America West Holdings Corp, said Antioco gained significant operational experience at the chain. Frank said Antioco was "successful" as CEO, and enhanced shareholder value.
While Antioco had a short stint at Taco Bell, Janice Meyer, an analyst at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette, said, "he pretty quickly grasped the issues at hand."
Meyer noted the fast food chain's first quarter same-store sales were up four percent after two years of declines.

"You can't credit that to one person," Meyer said. "It was a team effort. But John was a good leader, who very quickly grasped some of the issues facing Taco Bell," including a pricing strategy in the hotly competitive fast food industry.
